competencies.justification: Explaining key natural phenomena is the chapter's organising spine: 'The Complexity of Mapping the Earth' explains the oblate spheroid and projection distortion; 'The Blue of the Blue Planet, the Oceans' explains the ocean's role in regulating climate; 'Ocean currents' traces the Gulf Stream's effect on Western European coastal climate; and each continent section explains a formation process — the Tibetan Plateau by plate collision, the Urals by tectonic forces and erosion. Spatial distribution is carried by the tour announced in 'The Continents: Variety on Land', each section locating its landforms on a physical map. 'Before we move on …' names tectonic movements, erosion and deposition as the shaping processes. Without it there is no chapter.

'The Complexity of Mapping the Earth' is a self-contained section that could be taught as a lesson in its own right. Its subject is the representation and analysis of geographical data in map form: it establishes why every projection distorts, then has students compare the Mercator and Robinson projections. Its activity has students decode the colour language of physical maps, and that decoding is applied throughout — the Asia section sends students back to the colour key for Fig. 1.11, and the Tibetan Plateau section sets satellite images from 1987 and 2021 against each other. This is analysis of data given in tables, diagrams and maps, not passing illustration.

Indian perspectives on conservation are not met: 'The Continents: Variety on Land' states that India's landforms were covered in Part 1 and restricts the chapter to other parts of the world, leaving only the opening reference to Bhudevi and Vasudha, not a conservation perspective. Conservation and sustainability under global climate change runs as a deliberate thread, framed by the Big Question 'How do human actions trigger environmental issues?'. 'The Great Barrier Reef' closes on overfishing, pollution and climate change, stating that conservation is crucial; and 'Before we move on …' synthesises desertification, biodiversity loss and climate change into an argument for sustainable development. This keeps it short of the chapter's central focus.

Livelihood patterns are correlated with landforms, resources and climate across many named sections, and 'The Continents: Variety on Land' announces that the tour will examine each landform for 'in what ways they are connected to life'. The Gobi Desert section links harsh climate and sparse vegetation with seasonal herd migration; the European Plain links fertile soil with wheat, barley, rye and potato cultivation, and flat terrain with the growth of Moscow, Berlin, Paris and Warsaw; the Africa section links the Sahara with nomadic herding, oasis settlement and trade routes, and the Nile's irrigation with cultivation and hydroelectric power. The chapter's central focus lies elsewhere, in the physical features themselves.

Several named sections carry a passage whose subject is the distribution of raw materials and water across geographies: 'The Urals' closes on iron ore, copper, zinc, platinum, gold, coal, oil and natural gas; 'The Colorado Plateau' names coal, oil, natural gas, uranium and copper as the basis of the region's economic importance; and the Tibetan Plateau is identified as holding the largest freshwater reserves outside the polar regions. These are passages within landform sections rather than a dedicated section or self-contained activity block, and the chapter enumerates resource endowments as a closing beat without comparing distribution across geographies, so it is present but not a main focus.
